docs.title: Hugging Face
docs.extra: The GitHub of AI — models, datasets, and free live demos in one place. What it is: A giant public hub where anyone publishes AI models, datasets, and small web apps called Spaces. If a new model is open-weight, it almost certainly appears here first, with a page, docs, and usually a demo you can click right now. Why it matters: It removes the scariest beginner wall: you can try hundreds of models in your browser without installing anything, getting any key, or spending a cent. It's also where the local-AI ecosystem (Ollama, LM Studio) gets its models. Pricing: Free to browse, try demos, and download most models.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.extra: Where code lives — over 100 million projects, including most AI tools. What it is: The world's shared hard drive for code. Every AI project you hear about — Ollama, n8n, this website — has a repo here: the code, its full history, an issue tracker, and usually a README that explains everything. Why it matters: It's the closest thing tech has to a public library. Learning to search it, read a README, and 'star' things turns 'I heard about a tool' into 'I can actually run that tool'. Bonus: GitHub Actions gives free daily automation — which is how our freshness engine will run. Pricing: Free for public and private r

docs.title: OpenRouter
docs.extra: One API key → hundreds of models. The beginner-friendly front door to AI APIs. What it is: A single service that proxies almost every major model — the big closed labs and the open models — through one consistent API. One account, one key, one format; you can switch models by changing one string in your code. Why it matters: Beginners usually drown in five different developer portals before their first API call works. OpenRouter collapses all of that into one key and one endpoint — the fastest path from 'I have a key' to 'it replied!'. It also serves our Phase 2 price feed: their public model list includes live p

docs.title: Ollama
docs.extra: Run AI models on your own machine with one command. Free, offline, private. What it is: A small app for Windows/Mac/Linux that runs open-weight models locally. One install, one command ('ollama run <model>'), and you have a private ChatGPT-style chat with no account, no internet needed after download, and no per-message cost. Why it matters: It removes money and privacy from the list of beginner worries. Models run on YOUR machine: your notes, your files, your weird questions never leave it. It's also the best way to build an intuition for model sizes — 1B feels different from 8B on the same laptop. Pricing: Comp

docs.title: n8n
docs.extra: Visual automation: connect apps and AI without (much) code. What it is: A drag-and-drop canvas where you wire triggers ('new email arrives') to actions ('summarize with AI', 'save to a sheet'). Think of it as plumbing for apps — and AI is now one of the pipes. Why it matters: Most 'AI earns money / AI saves me hours' stories are really automation stories: AI does the thinking inside a pipeline someone built with a tool like this. Learning basic automation multiplies what one person can run alone. Pricing: Free self-hosted with your own computer/server. Cloud has a free trial then paid tiers.

docs.title: Google Colab
docs.extra: Free GPU notebooks in your browser — try AI code with zero installing. What it is: A hosted Jupyter notebook: code cells in a web page, running on Google's computers — including real GPUs. Write Python, press play, results appear. Nothing installs on your machine. Why it matters: GPUs are the expensive part of AI, and Colab lends you one for free. It's the standard place beginners run model experiments from tutorials — if a tutorial says 'open in Colab', that's the whole setup step. Pricing: Free tier includes time-limited GPU access. Paid tiers give faster GPUs and longer sessions.

docs.title: CapCut
docs.extra: Free, beginner-friendly video editor — the assemble step of most video and AI video workflows. What it is: A video editor (desktop, mobile, web) known for being the least painful way to cut clips, add auto-captions, drop in music, and export. AI video tools generate pieces; something still has to stitch the pieces together — usually this. Why it matters: Every AI video pipeline ends in an editor. CapCut's auto-captions alone save beginners hours, and its timeline-and-clips model teaches you editing basics that transfer everywhere. Pricing: Free tier does almost everything a beginner needs; a Pro subscription adds

docs.title: VS Code
docs.extra: The editor most developers use — now with AI helpers built in. What it is: Microsoft's free code editor: a fast, friendly notepad for code with a huge extension library. It's where you'll open, edit, and run almost everything you build. Why it matters: Beginners waste energy on editor debates that don't matter — the honest answer is: use VS Code. It opens any project (including this website's), runs terminals in a panel, and its AI extensions write half the boilerplate for you. Pricing: Completely free, open source.

docs.title: DaVinci Resolve
docs.extra: Hollywood-grade video editing and color — the free version has no real catch. What it is: The editor used on actual films, free for everyone. Edit on the timeline, fix colors like a colorist, clean audio — plus newer AI features (magic mask, voice isolation, auto subtitles in Studio). Why it matters: When CapCut starts feeling limiting, this is the natural next step that pros actually use — without a subscription. The cut page is simpler than it looks; the color page is what makes footage look 'expensive'. Pricing: The free version is genuinely full-featured (editing, color, Fairlight audio). One-time $295 for St

docs.title: Adobe Premiere Pro
docs.extra: The industry-standard video editor — now with text-based and AI editing. What it is: The editor most professional YouTubers and agencies run. Its 2025+ versions added AI text-based editing (edit video by deleting words from a transcript), auto captions, and generative extend. Why it matters: If you plan to work with clients or in a team, Premiere files are the shared language. Text-based editing is a genuine game changer for talking-head and interview content. Pricing: Subscription only (~$23/mo, or with the whole Creative Cloud). 7-day free trial.

docs.title: Filmora
docs.extra: Beginner-friendly editor with one-click effects and AI helpers. What it is: A consumer video editor that sits between CapCut and Premiere: timeline editing, a big effects/template library, AI smart cutout, AI music generator and auto captions. Why it matters: When you want pre-made transitions and title packs instead of building everything, Filmora's template library is the fastest path to a polished-looking video. Pricing: Free with watermark export; ~$10-20/mo or one-time license to remove it.

docs.title: Kdenlive
docs.extra: Fully free, open-source video editor — no watermark, no account, no limits. What it is: A community-built editor (runs on Windows, Mac, Linux) with timeline editing, effects, and auto-generated subtitles via whisper integration — with zero restrictions on the free version because there is only the free version. Why it matters: The honest 'forever free' option: no watermarks, no feature paywalls, no account. If a school, budget, or privacy stance rules out subscriptions, this is the real deal. Pricing: Completely free and open source (GPL). No pro tier, no upsells, ever.

docs.title: Descript
docs.extra: Edit video and podcasts by editing the transcript — delete words, not clips. What it is: An AI-first editor built around the transcript: the video is the text. Delete a sentence and the video cuts with it. Adds studio sound cleanup, filler-word removal ('um', 'uh'), eye contact correction and AI voice cloning for patching mistakes. Why it matters: For talking-head, tutorial, and podcast content it removes the hardest part of editing — nothing to learn about timelines. It's the fastest spoken-word pipeline in 2026. Pricing: Free tier: 1 transcription hour/month with watermark. Paid from ~$12-24/mo.

docs.title: Opus Clip
docs.extra: AI that turns one long video into ready-to-post shorts with captions. What it is: Upload a podcast/long video and the AI finds the most engaging moments, reframes them vertical, adds animated captions, and scores each clip's virality potential. Why it matters: Repurposing one video into 5+ shorts is the standard 2026 content strategy, and doing it by hand takes hours. This does the finding, cropping, and captioning in minutes. Pricing: Free tier: ~60 upload minutes/month with watermark. Paid from ~$15/mo.

docs.title: VEED
docs.extra: Browser-based video editor — captions, cleanup and quick edits, no install. What it is: An in-browser editor focused on the jobs beginners actually have: auto subtitles, text-to-video snippets, background noise removal, screen recording, and quick trims — nothing to install. Why it matters: Chromebook/school-laptop users and quick-fix editors can't install heavy apps. VEED covers 'trim this, caption that, clean the audio' in a tab. Pricing: Free tier with watermark; ~$12-25/mo removes it and unlocks AI tools.

docs.title: GPT family
docs.extra: Made by OpenAI. Best for: The safe default when you're not sure what to pick — the ecosystem around GPT models means almost every tool integrates with them. Context: Large context window; check the model page for the current size — it changes often. Strengths: General knowledge and instructions; multimodal understanding; huge ecosystem of tools built around it Weaknesses: Usage caps on free tiers; can be confidently wrong — verify facts Pricing: Free tier in the ChatGPT app; API is paid per token. docs.title: Claude family

Context: Known for very large context windows — long-document work is a signature use. Strengths: Writing quality and tone; careful reasoning; popular for coding help Weaknesses: Free tier message limits; less third-party tool coverage than GPT Pricing: Free tier in the claude.ai app; API is paid per token. docs.title: Gemini family
docs.extra: Made by Google. Best for: Multimodal work (video understanding, screenshots) and anyone living in Google Docs/Sheets/Gmail. Context: Very large context windows are a family trait — some variants ingest entire books and video. Strengths: Integration with Google's ecosystem; multimodal (video!) input; fast generous free tier Weaknesses: Naming/versioning is confusing; answers can feel inconsistent between versions Pricing: Generous free tiers in both the app and AI Studio. docs.title: GLM family
docs.extra: Made by Z.ai. Best for: Budget API projects and coding assistants; the open-weight versions make it a serious local-AI option. Context: Competitive context sizes; some variants specialized for coding and agent workflows. Strengths: Strong price/performance; coding and agentic variants; open-weight options for local use Weaknesses: Smaller beginner ecosystem than GPT/Claude; fewer third-party integrations Pricing: Known for aggressive pricing vs the big labs, with some open-weight releases. Live prices auto-arrive with the Phase 2 feed.

docs.title: Llama family
docs.extra: Made by Meta. Best for: Local, private, offline AI with Ollama — the 'ollama run llama3.2' experience is the on-ramp for a reason. Context: Varies by size; the small variants are designed to run on normal laptops. Strengths: The default local-AI family; sizes for every machine; huge fine-tune ecosystem Weaknesses: Behind the best closed models in raw quality; licensing has conditions for big commercial use Pricing: The weights are free to download — running them locally costs nothing but RAM. Hosted versions cost per token (Phase 2 feed covers prices).

docs.title: DeepSeek family
docs.extra: Made by DeepSeek. Best for: Cheap, good-quality API usage for text-heavy projects — and a benchmark for 'do I really need the expensive model?' Context: Large contexts; reasoning-oriented variants are the family's fame. Strengths: Famous price/performance; strong reasoning variants; open weights Weaknesses: Less polish in apps/UX; multimodal support behind the big closed labs Pricing: Made its name on extremely low API prices. Live prices auto-arrive with the Phase 2 feed.

docs.title: Qwen family
docs.extra: Made by Alibaba. Best for: Local models on modest hardware and multilingual projects — one of the best 'small model' lineups. Context: Varies by size; the many sizes make it flexible for local use. Strengths: Huge range of sizes and specialties; strong multilingual ability; open weights Weaknesses: So many variants it's hard to pick; app experience outside Asia is limited Pricing: Open weights free to run locally; cloud API is paid per token (Phase 2 feed covers prices).

docs.title: What even is an LLM?
docs.extra: The plain-English model of the model: what it actually does, why it's impressive, and the one thing people get wrong. Strip away the hype and a large language model is a text prediction engine. It has read a colossal amount of text, and it learned one skill extremely well: given some text, guess what comes next, one token at a time. That sounds too simple to be useful — until you notice that predicting the next word of a math solution, a translation, or a poem requires actually modeling those things. The prediction task forced the model to compress patterns of reasoning, facts, and style into itself. The key consequence: an LLM is a conversation partner, not a database. It doesn't look up an

docs.title: What is an API (really)?
docs.extra: The restaurant analogy, why JSON is the language, and what 'calling an API' looks like in practice. An API is a contract for programs to talk. You don't get to see inside the other program — you send a structured request to a fixed address (the endpoint), and it sends back a structured reply. The restaurant analogy holds up: you (your code) don't walk into the kitchen (their servers). You order from the menu (the API docs), the waiter (the API) carries your order in, and brings back your food (the result). You can't order anything not on the menu, and that's the point — a fixed menu is what makes it reliable. The menu language is JSON: labeled values in curly braces. A request to a chat mode

docs.title: Keep your keys safe
docs.extra: The 5 rules of API key hygiene — because one leaked key is one bad day. An API key is a password that can spend money. Everything below is just the habits that keep your bills boring. Rule 1 — keys live in .env files, never in code. Your code reads the key from the environment; the .env file sits in the project folder and is excluded from git with one line in .gitignore. (This project has it — steal our pattern.) Rule 2 — never paste a key into an AI chat, a screenshot, a 'funny bug post', or GitHub. Chat logs get saved; screenshots get shared; public repos get scraped by bots in minutes. Keys in any of those places should be treated as public immediately. Rule 3 — rotate on suspicion. Every

docs.title: API
docs.extra: A way for programs to talk to each other. When an app 'uses AI', it's usually sending text to a model's API and getting an answer back — like texting a very smart friend who always replies in a fixed format.

docs.title: API key
docs.extra: A long random password that proves it's you using a service. Keys can be free to get but billed per use — and must never be shared, posted, or committed to GitHub.

docs.title: token
docs.extra: The word-piece AI actually reads and writes. Models don't see letters, they see tokens — roughly 4 characters of English each. Limits and bills are counted in tokens, not words.

docs.title: context window
docs.extra: The model's short-term memory size, measured in tokens. Everything you and the model have said must fit inside it — past that, the earliest parts get forgotten.

docs.title: prompt
docs.extra: Everything you say to an AI. Good prompts are specific, give context, and say what format you want back — the same model gives wildly different answers to vague vs precise prompts.

docs.title: LLM
docs.extra: Large Language Model — the AI 'brain' trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token. ChatGPT, Claude, GLM and Gemini are different LLMs wearing different apps.

docs.title: open source
docs.extra: Code you can read, change, and run yourself. Free like a recipe is free — you still need a kitchen (compute) to cook it.

docs.title: open weights
docs.extra: The model's learned brain (its 'weights') is downloadable, so you can run it on your own machine. You can't change what it knows without retraining it, but you control where it runs.

docs.title: fine-tuning
docs.extra: Extra training on top of an existing model to change its behavior — its 'accent' and specialty, not its core knowledge. You don't rebuild the brain, you adjust it.

docs.title: RAG
docs.extra: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: grab the relevant documents first, hand them to the model with the question, so it answers from YOUR facts instead of guessing. The cheapest way to make AI accurate about your stuff.

docs.title: embedding
docs.extra: Turning text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so 'similar' becomes measurable math. How search systems find things by concept, not just keywords.

docs.title: inference
docs.extra: Running a trained model to get an answer — the 'using' phase, as opposed to the 'training' phase. Inference is what costs a little per question; training is what cost millions.

docs.title: GPU
docs.extra: The chip that makes AI math fast. Training big models wants thousands of them; using (running) a model can happen on one gaming GPU, a rented one, or even your laptop's CPU — just slower.

docs.title: quantization
docs.extra: Shrinking a model's numbers so it fits in less memory — slightly dumber, dramatically smaller. This is how big models run on normal laptops and phones.

docs.title: GGUF
docs.extra: The single-file format for local models used by tools like Ollama and LM Studio. Download one file, run one command — that's the whole local-AI experience.

docs.title: LoRA
docs.extra: A cheap way to fine-tune: train a small 'patch' instead of the whole model. Makes customizing a model possible on a single GPU for a few dollars.

docs.title: endpoint
docs.extra: The URL you send API requests to — an address for one specific skill of a service. Different endpoints do different jobs (chat, images, transcription...).

docs.title: JSON
docs.extra: A text format that's easy for programs to read: labels and values in curly braces. The language APIs speak — requests and answers travel as JSON.

docs.title: rate limit
docs.extra: A cap on how many requests you can send per minute or day, so one user can't hog the service. Hit the limit and you get a '429' error, not a bill.

docs.title: terminal
docs.extra: Type commands, computer obeys. It looks scary in movies, but it's just launching apps by typing instead of clicking — and the fastest way to run dev tools.

docs.title: git
docs.extra: A time machine plus save-points for code. Every 'commit' is a snapshot you can return to. Nearly every real project on Earth uses it.

docs.title: repository
docs.extra: A project folder tracked by git. On GitHub, a repo is a project's home page — with code, history, and a README explaining it.

docs.title: commit
docs.extra: A save-point in git with a short message describing what changed. Break something? Roll back to any commit and move on with your life.

docs.title: localhost
docs.extra: Your own computer pretending to be a server. http://localhost:4321 is a website only you can see — the safe playground before anything goes online.

docs.title: .env file
docs.extra: A file that holds secret keys separately from your code, so secrets exist in your project folder but never inside your code — and never on GitHub.

docs.title: PWA
docs.extra: Progressive Web App — a website that can install like a phone app and work offline. Same code as the site, zero app-store hassle.

docs.title: scraper
docs.extra: A small program that collects data from websites or APIs automatically — our 'freshness engine' is a set of polite scrapers that run daily.

docs.title: cron
docs.extra: A scheduler for computers: 'run this every day at 9am'. How the freshness engine updates while we sleep.

docs.title: CORS
docs.extra: Browser security rules about which websites may call which APIs. It's why some APIs work fine from an app but block a raw browser page — the site asks permission first.

docs.title: The tutor loop
docs.extra: Any new skill or subject. Turns a chat into an active tutor instead of a lecture.

docs.title: Explain it 5 ways

docs.title: Quiz me hard
docs.extra: Exam prep. Recall beats re-reading — this forces recall.
